kurals.tamil:
பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமைபா ராட்டுதல்
சுற்றத்தார் கண்ணே உள.
kurals.transliteration:
Patratra kannum pazhaimaipaa raattudhal
Sutraththaar kanne ula.
kurals.meaning: Even when a man has lost everything he owned, only his kin still honour the old bond they shared with him.
kurals.elementary: When someone’s pockets are full, lots of people want to sit next to them at lunch. But if they lose everything, most of those people drift away. Your family is different: they still remember the good times and stay by your side. That is what makes family special.
kurals.university: The chapter title சுற்றம் தழால் means ‘embracing the circle of kin’; Parimelazhagar glosses it as the king holding his kinsmen close so that they never leave him, and he explains that it follows ‘Selection and Employment’ (Ch. 52) because, having spoken of those who do the king’s work, Valluvar now turns to the rest of his ‘surround’. In this opening couplet பற்று means wealth or support, so பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் is ‘even when all holdings are gone’; the concessive உம் implies that such a man is normally no longer honoured by anyone. Parimelazhagar reads பழைமை as the kindnesses the man once did for them in his days of plenty, and the emphatic ஏ in கண்ணே stresses that kin alone keep faith, since others cut ties the moment the wealth is gone. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi all agree on the sense, and Karunanidhi turns it into a definition: those who show this loyalty are the true kin. Editions differ only in sandhi (உள / யுள) at the end of the second line.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama is stripped of his throne and sent into exile, his brother Bharata refuses the crown he has been handed, follows Rama into the forest to beg him to return, and then rules only as a regent, placing Rama’s sandals on the throne.
hinduism.explanation: Bharata stays loyal to Rama at the very moment when Rama has lost every worldly advantage, and he treats their old bond as more important than the kingdom.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the kind of kin the Kural describes, who honour the old tie even when the man has nothing left.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata’s visit to Chitrakuta and the sandals, sargas 100-115)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel of a kinsman’s loyalty to a dispossessed man, summarised in prose rather than quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says that a brother shows his real worth when trouble comes.
christianity.tie_back: Kin prove themselves in adversity, which is exactly the Kural’s point.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match: both texts single out the kinsman who stands firm when fortune fails.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Quraysh boycotted the Prophet’s clan and pushed them into the valley of Abu Talib for about three years, his uncle Abu Talib and the Banu Hashim, most of whom did not share his faith, kept protecting him out of kinship and went hungry alongside him.
islam.explanation: The clan stood by its kinsman when he had lost all outside support and was under economic siege.
islam.tie_back: This is kin keeping faith with one of their own when he has nothing, as in the Kural.
islam.source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (trans. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad), account of the boycott of Banu Hashim
islam._accuracy_note: Well-attested historical episode that fits kin loyalty in hardship; paraphrased, and the loyalty was tribal custom more than scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Ruth said: ‘Entreat me not to leave thee, and to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God;”
judaism.explanation: Naomi has lost her husband, her sons and her livelihood, yet her daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her.
judaism.tie_back: Ruth keeps the family bond alive when Naomi is widowed and has nothing, just as the Kural expects of true kin.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit; Ruth is kin by marriage, and the story focuses on personal loyalty more than on honouring past benefits.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “they do not forsake him in his troubles,”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the ways friends and associates repay a clansman who has treated them well; one is that they stand by him in misfortune.
buddhism.tie_back: Those who have been cherished do not abandon the man when trouble comes, which matches the Kural’s kin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit, but the sutta is talking about friends and associates rather than blood kin.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Polyneices dies attacking Thebes and is refused burial as a traitor, his sister Antigone buries him anyway and accepts death rather than abandon her disgraced brother.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antigone honours her kinship with a brother the whole city has rejected.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Only his kin stand by him once he has lost everything, as the Kural observes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong example of kin loyalty to a fallen man, though Antigone’s motive is religious duty to the dead rather than gratitude for past kindness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And in poverty and in other misfortunes men think friends are the only refuge.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that philia (the love of friends and family) matters most when fortune turns against us.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural gives this refuge specifically to kin, whose attachment outlasts a man’s wealth.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Aristotle’s philia covers kin as well as friends, so the match is good but broader than the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் இயையின் அருப்பறா
ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
ViruppaRaach chutram iyaiyin aruppaRaa
Aakkam palavum tharum.
kurals.meaning: If a man is blessed with kin whose love never fails, they will bring him many kinds of prosperity that keep on growing.
kurals.elementary: Think of a garden where lots of people help water the plants. The plants keep growing new branches and flowers. A family that loves you all the time works like those helpers: with them around, good things keep sprouting in your life.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar notes that விருப்பறா (‘whose affection never ceases’) is there to exclude kin who are secret enemies (உட்பகை), and that அருப்பறா qualifies ஆக்கம் to mean wealth that never stops putting out new shoots (அருப்பு, ‘sprouting’, which he glosses as கிளைத்தல், ‘branching’). This separates it from wealth that grows only by its owner’s own effort. He explains the conditional இயையின் (‘if one should obtain’) as a sign of how rare such kin are, and reads பலவும் (‘all the many’) as pointing to the six limbs of the state (army, subjects, treasury, ministers, allies and fortress), which keep growing because many hands tend them together. The couplet sets out the economic logic of the chapter: kin are the root of expanding prosperity. The text is stable, and the Tamil commentators agree on the meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Relatives, again, in consequence of mutual dependence and mutual aid, grow together, like lotus-stalks in a lake.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura warns Dhritarashtra that relatives who support one another flourish together.
hinduism.tie_back: Loving kin make prosperity grow together, which is the Kural’s அருப்பறா ஆக்கம், wealth that keeps sprouting.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close image of kin growing and prospering together through mutual aid, and it comes from a political-advice setting like the Kural’s.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher praises working together because it multiplies what each person gains and protects each of them.
christianity.tie_back: Bonds that never fail bring greater returns, as the Kural says loving kin bring wealth of many kinds.
christianity._accuracy_note: General praise of companionship rather than of kin in particular, but it shares the logic that bonds bring gain.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever loves that he be granted more wealth and that his lease of life be prolonged then he should keep good relations with his Kith and kin.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ties silat al-rahim, keeping up the bonds of kinship, directly to more provision and a longer life.
islam.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim: loving kin bring ever-increasing prosperity.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of kinship bonds leading to increased wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity!”
judaism.explanation: The psalm goes on to compare brothers living in harmony to fragrant oil and to the dew of Hermon, on which God commands blessing.
judaism.tie_back: Brothers united in affection bring down blessing, much as the Kural’s loving kin bring abundance.
judaism._accuracy_note: The psalm links kinship unity with blessing, though it speaks of divine favour rather than material wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sammodamana Jataka, a flock of quails caught in a hunter’s net rises together at their leader’s signal, lifts the net and escapes. They thrive while they stay in harmony, but once they start quarrelling they are all caught.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta’s fable teaches that a kin group in harmony prospers and is safe, and that discord ruins it.
buddhism.tie_back: Kin whose love never fails keep the whole group flourishing, which is the Kural’s point.
buddhism.source: Sammodamana Jataka (Jataka No. 33), trans. E. B. Cowell et al.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fable parallel on the benefits of harmonious kin; paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Castor is killed, his brother Polydeuces (Pollux) begs Zeus to let him share his own immortality with him, and the twins end up alternating their days between Olympus and the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: A brother’s unfailing love wins the twins a lasting shared blessing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Love between kin that never fails brings lasting gain, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Loose parallel: the reward is divine favour, not worldly prosperity.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that nature made brothers the way it made pairs of hands, feet and eyes, so that they could help each other, and that a man who treats his brother as a partner doubles his strength in every undertaking.
philosophy.explanation: For Plutarch, a strong bond between brothers is a practical asset that makes each brother more capable.
philosophy.tie_back: Affectionate kin multiply one’s resources, as the Kural teaches.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De Fraterno Amore (On Brotherly Love)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of Plutarch’s central analogy; paraphrased because the wording was not checked against a live text.

kurals.tamil:
அளவளா வில்லாதான் வாழ்க்கை குளவளாக்
கோடின்றி நீர்நிறைந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Alavalaa villaadhaan vaazhkkai kulavalaak
Kotindri neernirain thatru.
kurals.meaning: The life of a man who does not mix heart to heart with his kin is like a wide tank that fills with water but has no banks: whatever comes in simply runs away.
kurals.elementary: Imagine pouring water into a pond with no edges. The water spreads out and disappears, and the pond never stays full. A person who keeps away from family is like that pond: good things come, but with no one around to help hold on to them, they slip away.
kurals.university: The key word அளவளாவு means intimate mingling, literally ‘measuring together’. Parimelazhagar explains that heart-union grows out of exchanging one’s own measure with another’s, so the word stands by metonymy for close intimacy with kin, and ‘with kin’ is supplied from the chapter heading. குளவளா is the broad expanse of a tank and கோடு is its bank. For Parimelazhagar வாழ்க்கை here stands for the wealth that sustains life, and his point is that without kin to ‘hold’ it, a man’s wealth drains outward just as water spills from a tank that has no banks. He groups kurals 522-524 as showing kin to be the cause (ஏது), the fortress (அரண்) and the fruit (பயன்) of wealth, and this couplet shows kin as the fortress. Some printed texts divide the first word as அளவளாவு இல்லாதான், and thirukkural.net prints it with a space as அளவளா வில்லாதான்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And the tree that stands singly, though gigantic and strong and deep-rooted, hath its trunk soon smashed and twisted by a mighty wind. Those trees, however, that grow in close compact are competent owing to mutual dependence to resist winds more violent still.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells the king that a man cut off from his relatives is as easy to destroy as a lone tree in a storm.
hinduism.tie_back: The isolated man in the Kural is the bankless tank, and in Vidura he is the lone tree; both are defenceless without kin.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Nearly identical argument, made in a similar statecraft context, with a different image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is;”
christianity.explanation: The letter to the Hebrews warns believers not to drift away from the fellowship of the community.
christianity.tie_back: Drawing away from one’s own people is the very failure the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: About the religious community rather than blood kin, and it gives no economic reason.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favor of Allah upon you - when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together and you became, by His favor, brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an calls on believers to hold together and warns against splitting apart, since joined hearts are a divine favour.
islam.tie_back: Hearts joined together, like the Kural’s அளவளாவு, are what hold a community’s strength in place.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on joining hearts and avoiding division; the context is the religious community, not kin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hillel said: do not separate yourself from the community,”
judaism.explanation: Hillel’s maxim warns against cutting oneself off from the collective life of one’s people.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural pictures the man who stays apart from his kin as a tank with no banks, and Hillel names the same danger.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:4 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear parallel on the danger of isolating oneself, though Hillel means the congregation rather than one’s family.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Rukkhadhamma Jataka, the Buddha tells his quarrelling Sakya and Koliya kinsmen about a forest where the trees stood close together and survived a great storm, while a tree growing alone in the open was uprooted. The lesson he draws is that kinsfolk should stay united.
buddhism.explanation: The story shows kin standing together as protection against disaster.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s tank without banks and the Jataka’s lone tree both picture a life without kin as unprotected.
buddhism.source: Rukkhadhamma Jataka (Jataka No. 74), trans. E. B. Cowell et al.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic parallel told explicitly to kinsmen; paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the father and his quarrelling sons, the father asks each son to break a bundle of sticks, and none can. He then unties the bundle and shows how easily each stick snaps alone, teaching them that they are strong while united and easy to beat when divided.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable makes family unity the source of strength and separation the source of weakness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The single stick and the bankless tank both picture life without kin.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, The Father and His Sons (Perry Index 53)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Greek fable tradition rather than myth proper, but a close thematic match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “for no one would choose the whole world on condition of being alone, since man is a political creature and one whose nature is to live with others.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that even the happiest man needs people to share his life with, because humans are social by nature.
philosophy.tie_back: A life without close ties is empty however much it holds, just as the Kural’s tank stays empty however much water pours in.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good general match on human sociality; not specific to kin or to wealth draining away.

kurals.tamil:
சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படஒழுகல் செல்வந்தான்
பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற பயன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sutraththaal sutrap pataozhukal selvandhaan
Petraththaal petra payan.
kurals.meaning: The real reward of gaining wealth is to live in such a way that one’s kin gather round one.
kurals.elementary: Suppose you have a big box of snacks. If you eat them alone, it’s just snacks. If you share them, your cousins come and sit around you, laughing and talking. That circle of family is the real prize, not the snacks.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats sounds on purpose (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட, பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற) so that the verse itself seems to ‘surround’ its subject. Parimelazhagar glosses it as: the fruit a man gains from having gained wealth is to conduct himself, embracing his kin, so that he is encircled by them. He notes that in பெற்ற the final அ, and in அதனால் the particle அன், have dropped out for the sake of the rhyme. He explains that such conduct counts as the ‘fruit’ of wealth because it lets a king rule without enemies, and he treats it as the third term of the sequence cause–fortress–fruit (kurals 522-524). Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read it the same way. The gloss attributed to Mu. Varadarasan for this kural on thirukkural.net actually belongs to kural 468 and is evidently misplaced there.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn on liberality teaches that shared wealth lasts and wins companions, while hoarded wealth leaves its owner alone.
hinduism.tie_back: Wealth that gathers people round its owner is the Kural’s definition of what wealth is for.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in logic (wealth spent generously wins companions); the hymn speaks of the needy in general, not kin in particular.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes providing for one’s own relatives a basic duty of faith.
christianity.tie_back: Resources are meant to sustain one’s kin, which the Kural calls the very fruit of wealth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Framed as an obligation rather than as the purpose or reward of wealth, but clearly aligned.

islam.quote_or_event: “They ask you, [O Muhammad], what they should spend. Say, ‘Whatever you spend of good is [to be] for parents and relatives and orphans and the needy and the traveler.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an lists parents and relatives first among those on whom wealth should be spent.
islam.tie_back: Kin come first in the proper use of wealth, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on priority to kin; it says nothing of being surrounded by them as a reward.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Torah commands that when a brother becomes poor and his hand fails, his kinsman must uphold him and let him live alongside him, lending without interest.
judaism.explanation: The law treats supporting an impoverished relative as a duty of those who have means.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too sees the proper use of wealth as keeping one’s kin close and supported.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good parallel on using wealth for kin; paraphrased and framed as law rather than as the fruit of wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “performs the five oblations: to relatives, guests, the dead, kings, & devas. This is the fourth benefit that can be obtained from wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika the benefits to be gained from wealth, and offerings to relatives are one of them.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts define the benefit of wealth partly by what it does for one’s kin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in framing (the ‘benefits of wealth’), with kin as one of several recipients.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Telemachus reaches Pylos, he finds old King Nestor seated among his sons and people at a great sacrifice on the shore. His wealth is spent on feasting, and he is surrounded by a loyal household.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor is the Homeric picture of a prosperous old age: a rich king surrounded by devoted sons.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His wealth takes the form of kin gathered round him, the image the Kural holds up.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative scene rather than a teaching; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “even rich men and those in possession of office and of dominating power are thought to need friends most of all; for what is the use of such prosperity without the opportunity of beneficence, which is exercised chiefly and in its most laudable form towards friends?”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that prosperity is pointless without people on whom to use it for good.
philosophy.tie_back: The value of wealth lies in the people it gathers and serves, which is what the Kural teaches about kin.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-direct parallel on the purpose of wealth; Aristotle says ‘friends’, a term that includes kin.

kurals.tamil:
கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் அடுக்கிய
சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kotuththalum insolum aatrin atukkiya
Sutraththaal sutrap patum.
kurals.meaning: A man who can both give generously and speak kindly will be surrounded by kin, circle after circle of them.
kurals.elementary: If you share your crayons and also say nice things to people, everyone wants to be near you. Then their brothers and sisters come too, and soon there’s a big happy circle around you. Sharing plus kind words is like a magnet for family.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar notes that the verb ஆற்றின் (‘if one is able to accomplish’) stresses how hard it is to practise both virtues in due measure. He explains அடுக்கிய சுற்றம் as kin ‘stacked’ in succession: the kin of one’s kin, and then their kin, bound in a widening chain. He explicitly identifies the two means with the Sanskrit statecraft terms dāna (gift) and sāma (conciliation), the first two of the four upāyas, so this kural brings the Arthaśāstra toolkit into the domestic setting of kinship. Kurals 525-528, he says, set out the ‘means of embracing kin’. இன்சொல் (‘sweet speech’) links back to Chapter 10, இனியவை கூறல், and it anticipates the Buddhist saṅgahavatthu of giving and kind speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Straw (for a seat), ground (for sitting upon), water (to wash the feet and face), and, fourthly sweet words,--these are never wanting in the houses of the good.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura says that the houses of the good always have simple gifts for guests together with kind words.
hinduism.tie_back: Giving together with sweet speech is the Kural’s formula for drawing people close.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Pairs giving with sweet words, but the setting is hospitality to guests rather than winning kin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another; ... Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.”
christianity.explanation: Paul joins brotherly affection and courtesy with material generosity toward the community.
christianity.tie_back: Warmth together with giving is how the community holds together, much as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Both elements are present; ‘brotherly love’ is spiritual kinship.

islam.quote_or_event: “and to parents do good and to relatives, orphans, and the needy. And speak to people good [words] and establish prayer and give zakah.”
islam.explanation: The covenant verse joins material kindness to relatives with the command to speak good words.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s pair of giving and kind speech in one sentence, with relatives named.
islam._accuracy_note: Both virtues and kin are named together; the verse does not promise being surrounded by kin as a result.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who gives a peruta to a poor person receives six blessings, and whoever consoles him with words of comfort and encouragement receives eleven blessings.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yitzhak ranks kind, comforting words above even the coin that is given.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too joins the gift to the sweet word and treats both as essential.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 9b (William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Pairs giving and kind speech closely; the recipient is the poor rather than kin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are these four grounds for the bonds of fellowship. Which four? Generosity, kind words, beneficial help, consistency.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the saṅgahavatthu, the qualities that hold a family or community together, and the first two are giving and kind speech.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own formula: generosity and kind words bind kin around you.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the two methods and their binding effect.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before the war with the Titans, Zeus frees the Hundred-Handers, who are children of Earth like the gods themselves, gives them nectar and ambrosia and speaks to them respectfully to ask for their help. Won over, they fight on his side and secure his victory.
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus wins over powerful relatives by combining gifts with courteous words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Giving together with kind speech gathers kin as allies, as the Kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good structural match (gifts plus courteous words win kin allies); paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca insists that the manner of giving matters as much as the gift: a benefit given readily, with a kind face and gracious words, binds the receiver, while one given grudgingly or with harsh words loses its value.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, generosity and courteous speech together are what make a gift create lasting goodwill.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too requires both the gift and the sweet word.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of Seneca’s teaching on the manner of giving; it is not about kin specifically.

kurals.tamil:
பெருங்கொடையான் பேணான் வெகுளி அவனின்
மருங்குடையார் மாநிலத்து இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Perungotaiyaan penaan vekuli avanin
Marungutaiyaar maanilaththu il.
kurals.meaning: No one on this great earth has more kin around him than a man who gives freely and does not nurse anger.
kurals.elementary: Picture two kids. One shares a lot but gets angry and shouts all the time. The other shares and stays calm and kind. Everyone flocks to the second kid. Giving plus a calm heart brings the biggest family circle.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar glosses பெருங்கொடை as ‘great liberality’ of a kind that never itself leads to want. He takes பேணான் வெகுளி (‘does not cherish anger’) to mean that the king does not indulge anger beyond measure, since he grants that a ruler may sometimes need to show it. மருங்கு (‘side’) here means kin (கிளை), so மருங்குடையார் are ‘those who have people at their side’. This kural adds a negative condition to the positive means of 525: generosity will not keep kin if it comes with an unpredictable temper, a point that looks ahead to Chapter 31 (வெகுளாமை) and to 306, where anger is said to burn the raft of one’s own people (இனம்). The text is stable, and all the main commentators agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O king, anger is a kind of bitter, pungent, acrid, and hot drink, painful in its consequences: ... Do thou, O king, swallow it up and obtain peace.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura urges Dhritarashtra to master his anger so that peace can be restored within the Kuru family.
hinduism.tie_back: Restraining anger keeps kin together, which is the second condition in the Kural.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same setting (a king’s kin and anger); generosity is not the focus of this passage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another,”
christianity.explanation: Paul pairs putting away anger with active kindness toward others.
christianity.tie_back: Dropping anger and practising generous kindness is the combination the Kural says wins the widest circle of kin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear match on the anger half and a reasonable one on kindness; material generosity is not specified.

islam.quote_or_event: “So by mercy from Allah, [O Muhammad], you were lenient with them. And if you had been rude [in speech] and harsh in heart, they would have disbanded from about you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an credits the Prophet’s gentleness for keeping his followers around him, and says harshness would have scattered them.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says the same: a leader free of anger keeps his people close.
islam._accuracy_note: Striking match on gentleness keeping people ‘about’ a leader; generosity is implied rather than stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that a soft answer turns away wrath while a grievous word stirs up anger.
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts calm speech that defuses conflict with harsh words that inflame it.
judaism.tie_back: Setting anger aside keeps relationships whole, which is the Kural’s second condition.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches only the anger half and is paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that one should overcome the angry person by non-anger, the wicked by goodness, the miser by generosity and the liar by truth.
buddhism.explanation: The verse pairs non-anger and generosity as ways of winning people over.
buddhism.tie_back: Non-anger and liberality are exactly the two qualities the Kural names.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Both virtues appear together; paraphrased because the live text was not re-checked in this session.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phoenix tells Achilles the story of Meleager, who withdrew from battle in anger at his mother and refused the pleas and gifts of elders, priests, friends and even his own family, until his city was nearly lost.
greek_mythology.explanation: Meleager’s nursed anger cuts him off from his kin and nearly destroys his people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the reverse of the Kural: cherished anger drives kin away.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A negative example that illustrates the anger half; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch’s dialogue on controlling anger argues that anger, more than any other passion, makes a man hateful to those around him and drives away household and friends, while mildness makes him loved and approachable.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats mastery of anger as the key to keeping one’s household and friends loyal.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too makes freedom from anger a condition for having kin around one.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De Cohibenda Ira (On the Control of Anger)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Fair summary of the treatise’s thrust; not a verified quotation.

kurals.tamil:
காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும் ஆக்கமும்
அன்னநீ ரார்க்கே உள.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaakkai karavaa karaindhunnum aakkamum
Annanee raarkke ula.
kurals.meaning: A crow does not hide its food; it caws to call its kin and eats with them. Prosperity comes only to people of that same nature.
kurals.elementary: When a crow finds food, it doesn’t sneak off with it. It says ‘Caw! Caw!’ so its whole family comes to share. People who share like the crow end up with the most good things in life, because everyone sticks with them.
kurals.university: This is the best-known couplet of the chapter. Parimelazhagar explains that when crows find food they do not hide it (கரவா) but caw (கரைந்து) to summon their flock and eat together, and that the ‘prosperities’ (ஆக்கமும்) that come through kin belong only to those who have such a nature (அன்ன நீரார்). He lists those prosperities as freedom from enemies and great wealth. He reads the உம் in ஆக்கமும் as an ‘inclusive’ particle: such people gain not only virtue (அறம்) and pleasure (இன்பம்) but material wealth (பொருள்) as well. He defines the crow-like nature as arranging things so that kin enjoy everything one enjoys oneself. Some modern readers (e.g. Karunanidhi) take ஆக்கம் more broadly as ‘elevation’. The crow’s calling of its kin is proverbial in Tamil culture and is echoed in later didactic literature.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He feeds no trusty friend, no man to love him. All guilt is he who eats with no partaker.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn condemns the man who eats his food alone and shares it with no one.
hinduism.tie_back: The crow that calls others to its food is the opposite of the man who ‘eats with no partaker’.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.6 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close ethic of sharing food, with the negative case stated.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And all that believed were together, and had all things common; And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need.”
christianity.explanation: The first Jerusalem community pooled what it had and gave to each as they needed.
christianity.tie_back: Nothing is hidden and everything is shared, as with the Kural’s crow.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on sharing openly; the community is religious rather than kin, and prosperity is not promised.

islam.quote_or_event: “They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Ansar of Medina shared their homes and goods with the migrants, and the Qur’an promises success to those saved from stinginess.
islam.tie_back: Open-handed sharing leads to success, which echoes the Kural’s ‘prosperity belongs to such people’.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match of sharing with success; the bond is faith-brotherhood rather than blood kin.

judaism.quote_or_event: Isaiah describes the fast God desires as sharing one’s bread with the hungry, bringing the homeless poor into one’s house, clothing the naked, and not hiding oneself from one’s own flesh, that is, one’s kin.
judaism.explanation: The prophet treats open sharing with the needy, and never turning away from one’s own kin, as true piety, and promises that light and healing will follow.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Hide not thyself from thine own flesh’ is very close to the Kural’s கரவா, not hiding one’s food from one’s kin.
judaism._accuracy_note: Remarkably close on ‘not hiding’ from kin; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If beings knew, as I know, the results of giving & sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that anyone who understood the fruit of sharing would never eat without first sharing.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the crow’s rule: never eat without first calling others to share.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close ethic of sharing food; the fruits described are karmic rather than kin-based wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod advises the farmer to invite his friend to his feast, and above all whoever lives near him, because neighbours come running when trouble strikes while more distant kinsmen are slow to arrive.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod treats sharing one’s table with those around one as a practical way of building a circle that will help in need.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the crow, one calls others to share and so builds up support, though Hesiod ranks neighbours above distant kin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Right practice of inviting others to share, but it favours neighbours over kin; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For this cause it would seem that we ought to summon our friends readily to share our good fortunes (for the beneficent character is a noble one),”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle advises calling friends in readily to share one’s good fortune.
philosophy.tie_back: Calling others in to share one’s good fortune is exactly what the Kural’s crow does.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.11 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Striking match of ‘summoning’ others to share good fortune; Aristotle speaks of friends rather than kin.

kurals.tamil:
பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின்
அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Podhunokkaan vendhan varisaiyaa nokkin
Adhunokki vaazhvaar palar.
kurals.meaning: If a king does not treat everyone the same but gives each person the regard their merit deserves, many will stay by him because they value that recognition.
kurals.elementary: A good coach doesn’t give every player the same job. The fastest runner plays forward, and the one with the best hands becomes goalkeeper. When each person feels truly seen for what they’re good at, they all want to stay on the team.
kurals.university: The couplet contrasts பொது நோக்கு (‘common or uniform regard’) with வரிசை நோக்கு (‘regard according to rank or order’). Parimelazhagar reads வரிசை as each person’s own worth (தத்தம் தகுதி). He explains that uniform treatment is rejected because it drives away the superior, who feel slighted, while graded regard is prescribed because it keeps everyone loyal. This makes it a principle of proportional, not arithmetic, equality, very like Aristotle’s distributive justice. With this kural Parimelazhagar closes the four-verse unit (525-528) on the ‘means of embracing kin’. Karunanidhi’s modern gloss softens the hierarchy (‘all people are equal, but use each according to ability’), and Pappaiah places the kural explicitly within the ruler’s treatment of his kin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Laws of Manu list wealth, kindred, age, the performance of sacred rites and sacred learning as grounds for respect, each later one weighing more, so that honour is to be given by graded merit rather than uniformly.
hinduism.explanation: Manu sets out a scale for how much respect each person should receive.
hinduism.tie_back: This is graded regard (வரிசை நோக்கு) rather than uniform treatment (பொது நோக்கு), as the Kural prescribes.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallel principle of graded honour; paraphrased, and Manu’s criteria differ from the Kural’s merit-based view.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability;”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, the master entrusts each servant with a share matched to his ability.
christianity.tie_back: Treating each person according to capacity rather than uniformly is the Kural’s principle.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on proportional treatment; the parable is about accountability rather than keeping loyalty.

islam.quote_or_event: “And it is He who has made you successors upon the earth and has raised some of you above others in degrees [of rank] that He may try you through what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an treats differences of rank among people as part of the divine order and a test.
islam.tie_back: People are not all placed alike, so treating them according to rank reflects that order, as in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Only an indirect parallel: it describes divine distribution of rank, not a ruler’s policy of regard.

judaism.quote_or_event: At the end of his life Jacob gathers his twelve sons and blesses each one differently, according to his character and deeds; the text notes that he blessed every one according to his own blessing.
judaism.explanation: The patriarch does not bless his sons all alike but fits each blessing to the son.
judaism.tie_back: Individual rather than uniform regard among kin is exactly the Kural’s வரிசை நோக்கு.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel within a family; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Generosity, sweet speech, Helpfulness to others, Impartiality to all, As the case demands.”
buddhism.explanation: The closing verse of the Sigalovada lists the four ‘winning ways’ and qualifies them as applied ‘as the case demands’.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘As the case demands’ calls for the fitting treatment of each person that the Kural recommends.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Partial fit: ‘impartiality’ (samānattatā) seems to pull the other way, although ‘as the case demands’ supports fitting treatment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After defeating the Titans, the gods urge Zeus to rule, and he divides the privileges (timai) among them, giving each god a fitting share of honour, which secures their loyalty to his reign.
greek_mythology.explanation: Zeus keeps his divine kin loyal by giving each a distinct and appropriate honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is graded regard keeping the circle together, as in the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “To kinsmen, too, and fellow-tribesmen and fellow-citizens and to every other class one should always try to assign what is appropriate, and to compare the claims of each class with respect to nearness of relation and to virtue or usefulness.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that we owe different things to different people and must weigh each person’s closeness and merit.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s வரிசை நோக்கு, regard given to kin according to their worth.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.2 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, and it names kinsmen explicitly.

kurals.tamil:
தமராகித் தற்றுறந்தார் சுற்றம் அமராமைக்
காரணம் இன்றி வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thamaraakith thatrurandhaar sutram amaraamaik
Kaaranam indri varum.
kurals.meaning: Kin who were once close but left because of some grievance will come back of their own accord once the cause of the rift is gone.
kurals.elementary: Suppose your cousin stopped coming over because you kept teasing him. If you stop teasing, he’ll start coming back all by himself. When you fix the reason someone left, the friendship often heals itself.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar construes the couplet as: when those who were once one’s own (தமர்) have left because of some cause, their becoming kin again ‘comes’ (வரும்) of itself once that cause of discord (அமராமைக் காரணம்) no longer exists in oneself. He infers from the phrase that the cause really did exist before, and names it as the king’s own conduct, such as straying from the right path or doing things that displease. Because the kin were naturally affectionate and the estrangement was artificial, it ends when its cause ends; the ruler need not court them again, since they ‘return’ to their old nature. Pappaiah reads the kural in modern political terms, as members returning to a movement once the leader’s fault is gone. Karunanidhi reads it differently: those who left on some pretext come back once they see the pretext does not hold. Thirukkural.net prints தமராகிக் in the first word, but Parimelazhagar’s text on Wikisource and the standard editions read தமராகித், which is the reading adopted here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let, therefore, thy sons cherish the Pandavas, and the Pandavas also cherish thy sons. O king, let the Kurus and the Pandavas, both having same friends and same foes, live together in happiness and prosperity.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura urges Dhritarashtra to remove the cause of the family rift, his sons’ injustice, so that the estranged cousins can be reunited.
hinduism.tie_back: Remove the cause of the estrangement and the kin come back, as the Kural says.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 36 (Vidura’s counsel; trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Right setting (a king whose own side caused the rift with kin), but it is a plea rather than a statement of the principle.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”
christianity.explanation: The estranged son returns home and is welcomed without conditions.
christianity.tie_back: A kinsman who has left comes back and the old bond resumes at once, as the Kural predicts.
christianity._accuracy_note: The return of estranged kin matches, but here the fault lay with the son, not with the one who was left.

islam.quote_or_event: “Al-Wasil is not the one who recompenses the good done to him by his relatives, but Al-Wasil is the one who keeps good relations with those relatives who had severed the bond of kinship with him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet defines the true maintainer of kinship as the one who restores ties with relatives who have broken them off.
islam.tie_back: Keeping the way open for estranged kin to return is the spirit of the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on repairing broken kin ties; it puts the duty on the one who was left rather than predicting a spontaneous return.

judaism.quote_or_event: Twenty years after Jacob fled Esau’s anger over the stolen blessing, the brothers meet again, and Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, falls on his neck and kisses him, and they weep together.
judaism.explanation: Once the old grievance has faded, the estranged brother comes back and the kinship bond is restored.
judaism.tie_back: When the cause of estrangement is gone, kin return, as the Kural says.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel of reconciliation between kin; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Sakyas and Koliyas, kin connected by marriage, are about to go to war over the waters of the Rohini river, the Buddha removes the cause of the quarrel by asking whether water is worth more than the lives of princes. The kinsmen are reconciled.
buddhism.explanation: Once the cause of the dispute is set aside, the two kin clans return to peace.
buddhism.tie_back: Remove the cause and estranged kin come back together, as the Kural says.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verses 197-199; Kunala Jataka (Jataka No. 536), introduction
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good parallel of kin reconciled once the cause is removed; paraphrased from the commentarial tradition.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles withdraws from the Greek army because Agamemnon has insulted him by taking his prize Briseis. Once Agamemnon admits his fault and the grievance is set right in Book 19, Achilles returns to the fight.
greek_mythology.explanation: An estranged comrade returns once the leader’s wrong that caused his withdrawal has been removed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Remove the leader’s own fault and those who left come back, which is Parimelazhagar’s reading of the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good structural parallel, though Achilles’ return is driven mainly by Patroclus’s death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “so to those who have been our friends we ought to make some allowance for our former friendship, when the breach has not been due to excess of wickedness.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that a former bond still has a claim on us after a rift, provided the rift did not come from real wickedness.
philosophy.tie_back: An old bond whose rift has a removable cause can be restored, which is the Kural’s point.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Aristotle speaks of what we owe former friends, not of their spontaneous return; a reasonable but partial fit.

kurals.tamil:
உழைப்பிரிந்து காரணத்தின் வந்தானை வேந்தன்
இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uzhaippirindhu kaaranaththin vandhaanai vendhan
Izhaiththirundhu ennik kolal.
kurals.meaning: When a kinsman who left the king without cause comes back for some purpose of his own, the king should meet that need, wait, and weigh him carefully before taking him back.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a teammate who quit for no reason and now wants to rejoin because he needs something. The captain can help him, but should watch how he behaves for a while before trusting him fully again. Welcome back, but with open eyes.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar takes the bare உழைப் பிரிந்து (‘having left one’s side’) to imply that there was no reason for leaving, and காரணத்தின் வந்தானை as ‘one who came back because of some purpose’. He explains இழைத்திருந்து as ‘having done or supplied that purpose’: if the king does not meet the motive that brought the man back, he may leave again and join the enemy. He explains எண்ணிக் கொளல் as ‘accept him after examination’, because the man left without love and came back out of interest. Taken together with 529, Parimelazhagar sees two cases: the kinsman whom the king’s own fault drove away should be allowed to return freely, while the one who left without cause should be taken back only after scrutiny. Varadarasan similarly says the king should grant the help sought and then examine before re-admitting him, while Pappaiah reads இழைத்திருந்து as ‘waiting patiently’. Karunanidhi instead describes the man as one who left on a pretext and returned for a genuine reason.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Ravana’s brother Vibhishana deserts Lanka and comes to Rama asking for refuge, Rama first holds a council: Sugriva and others suspect a spy, and Hanuman argues from Vibhishana’s conduct and motive that he is sincere. Only after weighing their views does Rama accept him.
hinduism.explanation: Rama hears Vibhishana’s reasons, has him assessed and then takes him in, even promising him Lanka’s throne.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama both meets the man’s purpose and examines him before accepting, which is the Kural’s இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close procedural parallel (deliberate before admitting someone who came with a purpose), though Vibhishana is the enemy’s kin rather than the king’s own.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.”
christianity.explanation: Paul had refused to take John Mark on his second journey because Mark had earlier left the mission (Acts 15:37-39); years later, having seen him proven, Paul asks for him again.
christianity.tie_back: Someone who once left is taken back only after a period of testing, as the Kural advises.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good parallel of cautious then renewed acceptance; the relationship is a mission partnership, not blood kin.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘No blame will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful.’”
islam.explanation: Yusuf forgives the brothers who betrayed him, but only after testing them over several visits, including the planted cup, until he sees they have changed.
islam.tie_back: Taking back estranged kin after examining them is the Kural’s method.
islam._accuracy_note: The testing and then acceptance match well; the quoted verse gives only the forgiveness, with the testing in the surrounding narrative.

judaism.quote_or_event: When the brothers who sold Joseph arrive in Egypt needing grain, Joseph does not reveal himself at once. He tests them, holding Simeon and demanding that Benjamin be brought, and reveals himself and welcomes them only after Judah offers himself in Benjamin’s place.
judaism.explanation: The kin come back out of need, and Joseph examines them before restoring the bond.
judaism.tie_back: They come ‘for a reason’, their need is met with grain, and they are examined before being accepted, which is exactly what the Kural prescribes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The monastic code requires someone who formerly followed another sect and now asks to join the Sangha to live under a four-month probation (titthiya-parivāsa) so that his conduct and sincerity can be observed before he receives full ordination.
buddhism.explanation: The Sangha admits newcomers from rival groups only after a period of examination.
buddhism.tie_back: Accept the one who comes, but only after weighing him, as the Kural advises.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Procedural parallel of probation before acceptance; the applicants are outsiders rather than returning kin.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus returns after twenty years, Penelope does not take him back at once. She tests him with the secret of their bed, carved from a living olive tree, and embraces him only when he answers correctly.
greek_mythology.explanation: The one who has come back is carefully examined before being fully accepted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s எண்ணிக் கொளல, accepting only after deliberation.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates testing before acceptance, but Odysseus did not leave without cause.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Cicero’s dialogue On Friendship, Laelius advises that we should judge people before we give them our affection rather than love first and judge afterwards, and should test a character before trusting it.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero makes careful assessment come before full attachment.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s rule for the returning kinsman: examine first, then embrace.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Right principle of judging before trusting, but it is general advice about friendship; paraphrased.
